blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Millimeter-wave radar resolves the micrometer displacements of a moving body as micro-Doppler, enabling gait, gesture, activity, pose and vital-sign sensing. Each task relies on a downstream model trained on real data, yet radar datasets lag orders of magnitude behind vision and language. Brute-force collection will not close that gap, and existing synthesis methods (forward-only simulators, learned generators and static-scene inverse renderers) cannot fit a real capture of a moving body, leaving a sim2real gap. We present 4D Point Splatting (4DPS), a physics-based differentiable renderer that fits an explicit moving scene to a real capture. Using the synchronized camera to initialize the room and body, we represent the scene as oriented points carrying material, normal and velocity, and splat each point into range and Doppler bins. Our output is the raw complex return a real radar records, so we apply the same signal processing on the rendered data to obtain any representation for training any SOTA downstream model. We fit 235 sequences on HuPR and 100 on RT-Pose, two datasets with different radars. Our reconstructions set the state of the art, with median correlations of 0.940 and 0.830 on range-azimuth, 0.829 and 0.695 on range-Doppler, and 0.988 and 0.966 on micro-Doppler. Our renders also set the state of the art in downstream sim2real gap. On RT-Pose, a pose model trained on them reaches 21.9 cm MPJPE on real data, against 16.7 cm for real training and 127.6 cm for the RF-Genesis baseline, where both the rendered- and real-trained models learn nearly the same features. Our custom CUDA kernels fit a sequence in 5.7 minutes on HuPR and 12.9 on RT-Pose on one H100, making dataset-scale inverse rendering of mmWave radar possible for the first time. This work can enable synthetic data generation for any human-centered downstream task and model, and scene editing for data augmentation.
blocks.zh: 毫米波雷达可以解决移动体作为微多普勒的微米移位问题,使运动步态、姿态、活动、姿势和生命感知成为可能。 每项任务都依赖于接受过真实数据培训的下游模型,然而雷达数据集的量级却落后于视觉和语言. 暴力收集不会拉近这一差距,现有的合成方法(前方的唯模拟器,学习的发电机和静态-场面反向渲染器)无法符合对移动体的真正捕捉,从而留下一个sim2real差距. 我们呈现的是4D点电镀(4DPS),一种基于物理学的异构渲染器,它符合一个明显的移动场景,可以真正捕获. 使用同步摄像头来初始化房间和身体,我们代表场景为方向点,携带材料,正常和速度,将每个点都浮到射程和多普勒宾箱中. 我们的输出是原始复合体返回一个真实的雷达记录, 所以我们在提供的数据上应用同样的信号处理, 以获得任何用于训练SOTA下游模型的表示。 我们在HuPR上装了235个序列,在RT-Pose上装了100个序列,两个数据集有不同的雷达. 我们的重建设定了最新水平,在射程-半径上,中位相对比为0.940和0.830,在射程-多普勒上,0.829和0.695,在微多普勒上,0.988和0.966。 我们的制作还把最先进的技术 设定在下游的实实在在的差距。 在RT-Pose上,经过培训的模型在真实数据上达到21.9厘米MPJPE,而实际培训为16.7厘米,RF-Genesis基线为127.6厘米,其中制成型模型和经过实际培训的模型都学习了几乎相同的特征。 我们自定义的CUDA内核在5.7分钟的HuPR和12.9的RT-Pose上安装了一个序列,使mmWave雷达的数据集级反渲染首次成为可能. 这项工作能够为任何以人为中心的下游任务和模型提供合成数据生成,并进行场景编辑以进行数据增强。

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
Millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar resolves radial motion to a fraction of a
millimeter, works in darkness and through occlusion, and captures no
identifiable imagery ( Zhao et al., 2018 ; Guan et al., 2020 ; Adib et al., 2015 ) .
This makes it a natural sensor for privacy-preserving human sensing,
including gait, gesture, activity, fall and pose
recognition ( Lien et al., 2016 ; Singh et al., 2019 ; Zhao et al., 2018 ; Lee et al., 2023 ) . Each of these applications requires a downstream model trained
on real micro-Doppler ( Chen et al., 2006 ) , the phase modulation a moving
body imposes on the return. However, each is bottlenecked by the same data
scarcity, because public radar data lags orders of magnitude behind vision
and language corpora. Brute-force collection cannot close that gap:
radar sensors are rarer than cameras, and where a camera is point-and-shoot,
every radar capture needs a rig calibrated and synchronized to reference cameras
or LiDAR.

blocks.en:
Synthesis is the next best alternative, but every existing method leaves a
sim2real gap, because none fit to a real capture of a moving body.
Motion-driven simulators ( Sundar Ram & Ling, 2008 ; Vishwakarma et al., 2022 ; Chen & Zhang, 2024 ) carry geometry, materials and motion explicitly
but run forward only, so their parameters are set by an operator and never
optimized against a real capture. Learned generators such as
RF-Diffusion ( Chi et al., 2024 ) are trained on the same scarce data and keep the
scene implicit in network weights, so there is nothing to fit or edit. Radar inverse renderers do fit
real captures; mmIR ( Armouti et al., 2026b ) , 3DPS ( Armouti et al., 2026a ) and differentiable ray
tracers ( Hoydis et al., 2023 ; Hofmann et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2023 ) recover explicit materials and normals and render range,
azimuth and elevation. However, all currently assume a static scene and
evaluate one phase per point per frame so they have no slow-time axis (the
chirp-to-chirp axis along which Doppler is measured) and nothing along which
velocity could be defined. What is missing is a renderer that fits an
explicit moving scene to a real capture.

blocks.en:
We present 4D Point Splatting (4DPS), a physics-based differentiable
renderer that fits an explicit moving scene to a real capture, with velocity
as an estimated and differentiable parameter. Like prior radar
renderers ( Armouti et al., 2026b ; Armouti et al., 2026a ; Chen et al., 2026 ) , we initialize geometry from another
sensor, here the capture’s synchronized camera. We represent the scene as
oriented points, each carrying an ITU-R P.2040 material ( ITU-R, 2023 ) , a
surface normal and, for the body, a velocity, and we splat each point into
range and Doppler bins. The camera fixes where each surface is present but not how
strongly it reflects at millimeter wavelengths. That strength depends on the
surface’s material and on the angle between its normal and the radar, and it
sets the amplitude of every return. We therefore fit the materials, normals
and velocities by gradient descent until the rendered return matches the
recording (Fig. 1 , top). On HuPR, fitting raises the clutter-removed range–azimuth
correlation from 0.270 for the camera-initialized render to
0.666. Our output is the raw complex return that a real radar records,
for every chirp, antenna pair and range bin. We therefore apply the same
digital signal processing (DSP) to rendered and real data, and obtain any
representation, from range profiles to micro-Doppler, for any downstream
model (Fig. 1 , bottom). We validate each representation on two datasets with different array
geometries and downstream models.

blocks.en:
Introducing an explicit velocity into the forward model raises three
challenges. The first challenge is the cost: existing differentiable radar
renderers output one chirp per frame, so rendering Doppler would repeat that
render for every chirp, a cost that grows linearly with the chirp count and
rules out corpus-scale fitting. 4DPS instead splats each point into Doppler
bins as well as range bins (Fig. 2 ). A moving point’s return across
a frame’s chirps is a single tone, so its Doppler point spread function has a
closed form. Each point therefore deposits into seven Doppler bins instead of
being rendered 64 times. Second, ambiguity: velocity enters the forward model only through
a phase term that wraps every 2 ​ π 2\pi , so velocities one Doppler ambiguity
apart (9 m/s on HuPR) render identically, and gradient descent from an
arbitrary start lands in the nearest minimum rather than the true minimum. To address this, we initialize the joint velocities from the video’s kinematics and
learn only a residual, bounded by each joint’s own speed. Third,
supervision: one loss must train both the static scene and the person, who
holds a small fraction of a frame’s energy. A loss over the whole frame lets
a large relative error on the person hide behind the scene’s return, and a
loss on the person alone gives the scene no gradient. We therefore compare
the range–azimuth–elevation magnitude at two slow-time views: each frame’s
first chirp, which carries the static scene, and its Doppler planes, which
carry the motion. Each view is compared over the whole frame and over a
window on the person (Eq. 4 ). Solving these three problems lets us fit entire corpora for the
first time, with no manual input. We fit every usable sequence of both datasets,
235 on HuPR and 100 on RT-Pose, at about 5.7 and
12.9 minutes a sequence on one H100.

blocks.en:
We set the new SOTA in 4D range–azimuth–elevation–Doppler (RAED) tensor rendering and reconstruction, with median Pearson
correlations of 0.940 on range–azimuth and 0.988 on micro-Doppler
on HuPR, and 0.830 and 0.966 on RT-Pose
(Table 2 ). To test whether a model can learn from these
renders, we train each dataset’s official pose model on real or on rendered
data, four seeds each, and test it on both (Tables 3 and 11 ). Trained on
our renders alone, the models keep 0.59 of their real-trained
accuracy on HuPR and 0.76 on RT-Pose. By contrast, models trained
on RF-Genesis renders of the same motion fail on real data, at
1.8 AP on HuPR and 127.6 cm MPJPE on RT-Pose.
Because our rendered-trained models score far higher on renders than on
recordings, the gap that remains is realism rather than missing information.
A comparison of the two models’ internal representations shows that they
compute the same features from the backbone onward (Sec. 4.3 ).

blocks.en:
Contributions. In summary, we make the following contributions: 1) 4DPS, to our knowledge
the first differentiable renderer of human micro-Doppler: oriented points
carrying material, normal and a velocity estimated per joint for the first
time, splatted in closed form into range and Doppler bins, rendering the raw
complex return so any representation follows; 2) a range–Doppler point
splatting framework, with a closed-form Doppler point spread function and
Doppler-resolved supervision, that makes corpus-scale inverse rendering
tractable across multiple public corpora and different array geometries for
the first time; 3) the first sim2real analysis
of radar inverse rendering on downstream models: the real/rendered
train–test matrix for radar human pose on two datasets with the official
models, and an interpretability analysis showing that rendered- and
real-trained models learn the same features; and 4) release of the
renderer, the fitting chain, every fitted scene and rendered cube, the
mesh-derived RT-Pose labels, the retrained models and the evaluation suite,
on acceptance.

blocks.en:
Differentiable radar rendering. Radar-domain renderers fit explicit scene parameters to
captures. Differentiable ray
tracers ( Hoydis et al., 2023 ; Hofmann et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2023 ) do so on synthetic or known-geometry scenes.
mmIR ( Armouti et al., 2026b ) fits the raw ADC of real captures and recovers materials,
normals and antenna patterns, and 3DPS ( Armouti et al., 2026a ) replaces mmIR’s Monte
Carlo sampling with closed-form point splatting. Every one of these
renderers reconstructs a static scene. Its forward model evaluates one phase
per primitive per frame, so it has no slow time, the axis along which Doppler
and velocity are defined. 4DPS renders that axis in closed form and
estimates velocity, so it fits a moving scene (Table 1 ).

Radar data synthesis. Radar ports of neural fields and Gaussian splatting ( Huang et al., 2024 ; Borts et al., 2024 ; Kung et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ; Rafidashti et al., 2025 ) supervise on post-FFT
power and discard phase, so they cannot render the phase that encodes
micro-Doppler. DART ( Huang et al., 2024 ) is the only one with a Doppler axis,
and its Doppler comes from ego-motion, not from an articulated subject. Motion-driven
simulators ( Sundar Ram & Ling, 2008 ; Vishwakarma et al., 2022 ; Chen & Zhang, 2024 ) produce human micro-Doppler but run forward
only, so their residual against a real capture is either never quantified or never minimized.
mmGPE ( Xue et al., 2023 ) narrows that residual with a learned refiner on the
simulator’s output, without fitting the scene. Learned
generators ( Chi et al., 2024 ) leave the scene implicit in network
weights, where nothing can be fitted or edited. Concurrent with this work,
HybridSim ( Xiong et al., 2026 ) ray traces a physics-learning hybrid over
eight sequences from one single-chip radar, trained end to end with the

makes of it. An RF-Genesis render holds the person alone and carries little
of the limbs’ micro-motion (Sec. 4.1 ), so a model trained
on it never learns to separate a moving body from the room around it. The
4DPS renders do carry the pose information a model needs. Tested on held-out
renders, a 4DPS-trained model scores 59.6 (1.4) AP and 15.71 (1.38) cm,
close to the real-trained model on recordings
(Table 11 ). Its drop
on recordings therefore comes from the remaining rendered–real
differences, which the model first meets at test time. Per
keypoint, the drop concentrates in the arms (Fig. 4 ,
right). On HuPR the wrists fall from 22.2 and 25.1 AP to
8.0 and 4.7, while hips, knees and the head keep

blocks.en:
HuPR is the harder downstream task of the two, although its renders score
higher on fidelity (Table 2 ), for three reasons. i) One sequence gives the
renderer 921,600 chirps against RT-Pose’s 3,674,112, a factor
of 0.25. ii) Its radars also resolve the lateral axes far more
coarsely. Eight azimuth elements on a single chip put the broadside resolution
near 14.3 ∘ , against 1.3 ∘ for the cascade’s 86
slots. Each HuPR board resolves one axis only, azimuth on the horizontal and
elevation on the vertical, and carries 2 elevation bins where the
cascade carries 8. The labels, meanwhile, are keypoints in a camera
image whose pixels subtend about 0.2 ∘ . The model must place
joints on a grid some seventy times finer than its own sensor
resolves laterally. iii) Coarse angles make the camera-to-radar extrinsic
harder to estimate as well, and our fit is sensitive to that registration, as
prior radar inverse renderers are ( Armouti et al., 2026b ; Armouti et al., 2026a ) (App. I ).

blocks.en: 4.3 Comparing Real- and Rendered-Trained Models
blocks.zh: 4.3 比较实际和招标培训模式

blocks.en:
Does a model trained on renders learn the same features as one trained
on real data? We compare the two models’ activations layer by layer with two standard similarity measures, orthogonal
Procrustes distance ( Williams et al., 2021 ) and debiased linear
CKA ( Kornblith et al., 2019 ; Nguyen et al., 2021 ; Murphy et al., 2024 ) , because no single
measure wins across settings ( Klabunde et al., 2025 ) . Each distance (Procrustes, 1 − 1- CKA) is divided by that between two of five real-trained
models, which differ only in seed,
so 1.0 means as similar as two real-trained models, and we fixed 1.2 1.2 as the
margin before running the analysis (Table 4 ). The Procrustes
ratio stays between 0.98 and 1.05 at every layer on
RT-Pose and between 1.05 and 1.17 on HuPR, and CKA
clears the margin with confidence only at RT-Pose’s first layer
(1.35), where the rendered and real inputs themselves differ most.
Training on renders therefore teaches the same features as training on real
data, consistent with Sec. 4.2 , where the rendered-trained
model’s drop comes from rendered–real differences in its input. Features that look alike can still serve pose estimation differently, so
we also freeze each model’s feature extractor and fit a new linear pose
readout on real data. On HuPR, features learned from renders give
1.30 times the keypoint error of real-trained features,
against 2.50 times for an untrained network. Therefore, they
carry most but not all of the pose information. At the
deepest layers even an untrained network scores about as close
( † ), so similarity there is no evidence either way.
App. F gives every layer, the error-consistency analysis
and the protocol.

blocks.en: 5 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 5 结论

blocks.en:
We presented 4DPS, a physics-based differentiable renderer that fits an
explicit moving scene to a real radar capture. Camera-initialized oriented
points carry an ITU-R P.2040 material, a normal and a velocity, and are
splatted in closed form into range and Doppler bins on the TDM timing of a
MIMO array. The closed-form Doppler splat makes the fit cheap enough to run
unattended over all 235 HuPR and 100 RT-Pose sequences, and
because 4DPS renders the raw complex return, the real data’s DSP turns it into
any representation. 4DPS sets the state of the art on range–azimuth,
range–Doppler and micro-Doppler. On HuPR it reaches median correlations of
0.666 on clutter-removed range–azimuth and 0.988 on micro-Doppler,
against 0.339 and 0.671 for RF-Genesis driven by the same motion.
Pose models trained on our renders alone keep 0.59 of their
real-trained accuracy on HuPR and 0.76 on RT-Pose, while models
trained on RF-Genesis renders do not transfer. The rendered- and real-trained
models also compute the same features, so the remaining gap comes from
rendered–real differences in their input. Limitations and future work. Velocity stays within a bounded
residual of the video kinematics. The background is static and rendered along
single-bounce paths, and we model one person per sequence. RT-Pose’s labels
come from the body mesh that drives the render, and no public simulator takes
a capture as input, so our baselines run forward
(App. I ). Scoring edited scenes against real
recordings is the next step (App. G ).

HuPR scaffold. Frames 0, 150, 300 and 450 of the sequence are read
from the released RGB, passed in one batch through Depth-Anything-V2
(Large, metric) ( Yang et al., 2024 ) , the annotated person’s bounding
box (padded by 12%) is cut out of each depth map, and the maps are
back-projected under a 52 ∘ 52^{\circ} horizontal field of view, estimated from the radar’s range and the released 2D keypoints, at a
pixel stride of 2, voxel-downsampled at 4 cm per view and 5 cm after
merging, and given PCA normals (0.18 m radius, 50 neighbors) oriented
toward the radar. Two person-free real maps are formed per board: the initial
material fit trains on the pixelwise median of the four sampled frames’
loop-mean | RA | |\mathrm{RA}| , and the range alignment scores against the
per-cell 25th percentile of loop-mean | RA | |\mathrm{RA}| over every fourth frame
of the sequence (the subject is the only mover and occupies any one cell in
a minority of frames, so a low quantile is the static scene with the person
gone). The range translation is searched on a 2 cm grid over ± 2.4 \pm 2.4 m and
refined at 2 mm, every candidate scored at once on the GPU (0.3 s): the
score is the min–max-normalized Pearson correlation of the shifted cloud’s
(range, angle) occupancy against the person-free map, mean over both boards,
restricted to the cloud’s own angle bins (the camera sees ± 26 ∘ \pm 26^{\circ} of
the radar’s ± 75 ∘ \pm 75^{\circ} ) and to ranges beyond 0.5 m. Lateral offset and
height are not fitted because the map constrains them poorly: positions
within 0.03 of the best score span a median of 1.3 m laterally and 1.0 m in
height, while the range optimum has no rival within 0.03 on 233 of 235
sequences: sequence 256: − 0.55 -0.55 m ( r r 0.23 to 0.49);
38: − 1.11 -1.11 m (0.10 to 0.48); 102: − 0.77 -0.77 m (0.13 to 0.57). The point-cloud
initialization of Armouti et al. (2026a) then reduces the aligned cloud to N = 20,000 N=20{,}000 points by a
field-of-view restriction, cosine-weighted resampling toward boresight and
farthest-point sampling, and fits per-point materials and normals to the
person-free static | RA | |\mathrm{RA}| of both boards for 75 iterations
(2–3 s), the trainer refining both for its 400 epochs.

to the cloud. r f r_{f} moves the body along its centroid’s camera ray to r f r_{f} times its

blocks.en:
Table 6 records the mmWave human-sensing datasets we

blocks.en:
Two failure modes dominate. The first is the on-chip CFAR and beamforming
pipeline discarding slow time before release, which removes every dataset in
the table’s second section. The second is withholding camera imagery for
privacy, a practice that is tightening rather than relaxing. Only RT-Pose ( Ho et al., 2025 ) and HuPR ( Lee et al., 2023 ) satisfy all six criteria.

表格的第二节。 二是截取相机图像
隐私,这是一种收紧而不是放松的做法。 只有RT-Pose(Ho等人,2025年)和HuPR(Lee等人,2023年)符合所有6个标准.

blocks.en:
One terminology caveat carries into the rest of the paper. “Raw” is used
inconsistently in this literature, and HIBER ( Wu et al., 2023 ) , MMVR ( Rahman et al., 2025 ) ,
and M4Human ( Fan et al., 2026 ) all describe beamformed tensors as raw radar data.
Only ADC or I/Q samples preserve the per-chirp phase history that micro-Doppler
is computed from.

blocks.en:

as of 3 August 2025) on all 335 sequences that 4DPS renders, on both
datasets, and no sequence failed. Each sequence is driven by the registered

is scored by the same code on the same pose-speed frames
(App. D ), so the two rows of Table 2 differ only in the renderer.

blocks.en:
Changes to the released code. Each change is needed for the output to
describe our radar and the recorded motion, and none adds a fitted parameter:
(i) the camera and the spot light that stands for the transmitter sit at the
radar board, along its boresight; (ii) the registered mesh’s vertices replace
the text-generated motion; (iii) the ray intersection is evaluated before the
render call, which changes no value but lets the pipeline link on our driver;
(iv) each chirp is timed at its slot in the recording’s TDM schedule and fires
its own transmitter, where upstream spread the chirps over the whole frame and
so scaled every Doppler frequency by 3.6 × 3.6\times ; and (v) the interpolator
reads the depth channel where it read intensity as depth.

and model pairs.

blocks.en: G.2 Novel motions
blocks.zh: G.2 小说动议

blocks.en:
Source and placement. Data augmentation for new activities and for falls needs motions that neither
dataset contains, so we render such motions in fitted scenes. We take jumping jacks, squats, kicks and one real
fall, a rug pulled from under the subject, from the CMU motion-capture set in
AMASS ( Mahmood et al., 2019 ) . CMU has no clean forward or backward fall, so we generate those two with
MDM ( Tevet et al., 2023 ) , a text-to-motion model trained on HumanML3D ( Guo et al., 2022 ) . MDM’s samples
often end in a different posture from their prompt. We therefore drew three samples per prompt and kept the one
whose joints do what the prompt says. We judge that by the pelvis’s travel relative to the radar and by where the
toes point at the end. Each clip is labeled by that measured outcome. We pose each clip with the body shape fitted to the
scene’s own subject and resample it to the radar’s 10 Hz frame rate. We then place it on the scene’s floor at the
subject’s real position, facing the radar. No scene point more than 15 cm above the floor may come within 5 cm
of the body in any frame. Where the subject’s own position fails that check, we move the start to the nearest
point within 1 m that passes, which moved 7 of the 6 × \times 5
renders by at most 0.9 m. The render then follows App. G.1 : the
scene, its materials, noise floor and gain, and the subject’s person material come from the fit. The velocities
are the clip’s joint kinematics scaled by the subject’s fitted per-joint factors. A motion without a recording
has no per-frame velocity correction to fit, so these renders carry the motion fidelity of a render without the
velocity fit.

blocks.en:
Is every term of the objective necessary? Four terms at unit weight
invite the question. We therefore remove each global term alone and the two windowed
terms together. The windowed pair shares one window and one scope, the
person’s box, so we remove it as one unit. We expect the global loop-0 term to
matter most. The plane terms exclude DC and the windowed pair reaches only the
person’s box, so the global loop-0 term is the only term that reaches the whole
static scene. Each variant multiplies the removed terms by
zero inside the loss and re-fits the renderer once per sequence, with
everything else at the default configuration (the same epochs, person inputs,
scaffolds and seed). The “None” row is not a re-fit. It is the
render Table 2 reports, and it reproduces
Table 2 and

Table 2 ’s sequences (HuPR 235 per board, RT-Pose
63 one-person). The gap to real, rendered-to-real minus
real-to-real paired per sequence, is read through the four real-trained seeds
that Table 3 reports, and only on the test splits (HuPR
21, RT-Pose 13 sequences), because the
real-trained models are in-sample on every other sequence. We also count, per
sequence and radar, how often a variant scores worse or better than the

renderer seed, because sequences rather than seeds are the axis we generalize
over. Only the medians and the paired counts are therefore interpretable, never
a single sequence.

blocks.en:
The training step. Three decisions make a corpus-scale fit affordable. First, the step has no
data-dependent shape and no host synchronization: the path count is fixed per
step and the loss chain and frames are batched, so the whole training step is
captured once as a CUDA graph and replayed. Second, the forward model runs in
fused CUDA kernels with hand-written backward passes, and the Doppler-plane
amplitudes are evaluated in closed form (Eq. ( 16 )). Third, everything in Eq. ( 3 ) that does not
read a normal or a material is cached per frame, for the scene and for the
person’s paths, and the person’s paths are sorted once per frame by their
target cell, so each accumulator cell is one contiguous run summed without
atomics.

blocks.en:
Single-bounce transport, and one mover. As in prior radar
splatting ( Armouti et al., 2026a ; Kung et al., 2025 ) , we render the single-bounce path
from each transmitter to a point and back, so the returns that reach a receiver
only after reflecting off a second surface are absent from every product. Only
the subject moves: the scene is fitted once per sequence and held static, and
one person is modeled, because RT-Pose annotates the pose of only one person
in its multi-person sequences. Its 37 two-person sequences are
therefore fitted against the annotated person alone, and the paper reports
results on the one-person sequences.

Motion and labels come from the video’s body model. Each point’s
velocity stays within a bounded residual of the kinematics the monocular body
model supplies, and the skeleton comes from that model, never from a radar
label. The fit therefore corrects the video’s motion rather than recovering
it independently: a limb the body model misplaces beyond the bound is a limb
the radar term cannot invent, and the bound is what keeps the Doppler fit from
absorbing scaffold error as spurious velocity. RT-Pose’s labels are derived on
every radar frame from the same registered mesh that drives the render, with
the released-label result reported beside them (App. E ).

Elevation is the weakest axis. The scaffold reconstructs elevation
least well of the three spatial axes, because it is built from a monocular
depth or LiDAR scene and a body model rather than measured by the radar. The
products that resolve elevation are therefore the harder ones, which is why
HuPR’s vertical board and the RT-Pose cascade score below HuPR’s horizontal
board throughout Sec. 4.1 . Two of HuPR’s encoder taps are
also undefined in the representation analysis, because the temporal merges
feeding them are denormal in some trained checkpoints
(App. F ).

cannot show what a competing fitted renderer would achieve. The survey in

What the equivalence measurements cannot settle. An equivalence claim
needs a control that detects a difference of a known size, and the only one we
trained is the untrained network. It separates cleanly at the shallowest taps
and barely at all at the backbone output and the head, so the pre-registered
margin means less the deeper the tap, and we read the two deepest taps as
degenerate rather than as passes. We also did not train a second real arm per
seed from a shared initialization, so the same-initialization row is read
against the different-initialization real–real mean rather than against a
reference of its own (App. F ).

the two datasets differ in radar geometry, in downstream architecture and in
label provenance at once, so this evaluation cannot attribute the difference
